Essay

The SC on June 11, 2026 held that unpaid domestic labour performed by Housewives must be assigned an independent economic value while determining compensation in motor accident death cases, they are accidents involving motor vehicles—such as cars, buses, trucks, motorcycles, or autorickshaws—that cause injury, death, or property damage. It fixed minimum notional income 30000 per month.

Home makers are Nation builders.

Care work includes childcare, elderly care, supporting persons with disabilities, nutrition, health management and emotional support within households. Though often unpaid and invisible in economic statistics, it directly contributes to human capital formation by improving health, education, skills and productivity.

Well-nourished and adequately cared-for children are more likely to develop better cognitive and physical capabilities, perform well in education and become productive members of the workforce. Similarly, care for elderly and dependent persons supports the well-being of the entire household.

Thus, unpaid care work creates a social and economic foundation for future productivity. Recognising, reducing and redistributing this work through childcare facilities, healthcare services, social protection and greater sharing of household responsibilities can strengthen both human capital and inclusive economic growth.

Created distinct head of compensation called "loss of domestic care" in motor accident claims and mandated a 10% increase in this amount every three years.

The ruling came in an appeal from a motor accident claim in Punjab.

Observing that welfare-oriented objective of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, India’s principal legislation regulating motor vehicles, road transport and traffic. It covers vehicle registration, driving licences, permits, insurance, road safety, offences, penalties and compensation for victims of motor accidents, is frustrated when compensation claims remain pending for years.

SC says – Cooking, cleaning, caregiving etc play vital role in contribution of GDP.

Therefore, Home makers are architects of India's human capital. It recognised unpaid domestic work as a measurable economic contribution.

Methods of Valuing Unpaid Domestic Work:

Unpaid domestic work can be valued through three major methods: Replacement Cost Method, which estimates the cost of hiring workers for similar services; Opportunity Cost Method, based on income forgone by the homemaker; and Output Method, which estimates the monetary value of goods and services produced within the household.

Court noted that women spend over seven hours a day on unpaid domestic tasks, nearly 2.6 times more unpaid caregiving work than men and contribute an estimated 15–17% of India's GDP through this labour. That figure appears nowhere in the national accounts. Conventional GDP measurement excludes household production entirely.

For the life insurance industry, the ruling is an instruction it should act on without waiting for a regulatory directive. The Court limited the home maker definition to women only; if a man does the same, what next? and an unemployed job seeker between placements or yet to enter employment these are also "non-earning woman performing domestic work".

Unpaid Work and Female Labour Force Participation:

The unequal burden of unpaid domestic and caregiving work can constrain women’s participation in the formal labour market. Time spent on cooking, cleaning, childcare and elderly care reduces the time available for paid employment, education and skill development. This can contribute to career interruptions, lower earnings and economic dependence. Improving access to childcare, healthcare, sanitation, water supply, safe transport and flexible work arrangements can reduce this burden and enable greater workforce participation. Thus, recognising and redistributing unpaid work is important for women’s economic empowerment, inclusive growth and human capital development.
